India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here.
  • Recent findings suggest that the 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India.
  • India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here.

Recent findings suggest that the 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.

India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.

So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.

My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.

‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’.

One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.

Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.

The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.

Recent findings suggest that the following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.

For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.

Recent findings suggest that walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.

Sources indicate that the trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she remarked. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.

‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’.

The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.

Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.

Industry observers note that but the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” claims Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.

Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she states, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.

Recent findings suggest that travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.

Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.

Sources indicate that discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.

Sources indicate that politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry stated that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.

Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.

Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.

A recommendation from someone with great taste.

It has been revealed that shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the substantial streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”.

Sources indicate that firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.

Sources indicate that AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI manufacturer. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.

The Latest Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

In a recent development, the retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also noted it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

Sources indicate that "The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time.".

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the organization performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Industry observers note that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the tech giant said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The organization stated it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength revealed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

It has been revealed that as it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The substantial-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer noted on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A record number of children were living in a conflict zone in 2025, Save the Children findings revealed on Thursday.
  • It has been revealed that in the latest report in the "Stop the War on Children" series, the humantarian group said 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones.
  • "For millions of children, fear, violence and displacement are part of every day life," noted Save the Children Germany CEO Florian Westphal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A record number of children were living in a conflict zone in 2025, Save the Children findings revealed on Thursday.

It has been revealed that in the latest report in the "Stop the War on Children" series, the humantarian group said 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones. That's the highest number since records began in 1990, and more than double the total in the mid-1990s.

"For millions of children, fear, violence and displacement are part of every day life," noted Save the Children Germany CEO Florian Westphal.

He remarked this needed to be a "wake-up call" for the international community.

According to recent reports, around two in five children in both Africa and the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025, the report found. Africa, alone, accounted for 44% of all children living in conflict zones worldwide.

In terms of regional proportions, 40.2% of children in the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025. That represented roughly two in five children across the region, and a particularly steep rise in the number of children affected. The figure jumped by nearly 29% from 52 million in 2024 to 67 million last year.

Children's exposure to conflict in Africa has more than tripled over the past 15 years, with the share of children living in conflict zones rising from 12% in 2010 to 39% in 2025.

The report highlighted the dramatic increase in the denial of humanitarian access.

A total of 8,322 verified incidents of denying access to humanitarian aid to children were recorded in 2025, a 16-fold rise over the past decade. The figure was 509 in 2015, and only eight incidents were reported when the United Nations (UN) established the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in 2005.

The Palestinian Territories accounted for the vast majority of cases, with 5,946 incidents, or more than 70% of all verified cases globally.

"No grave violation has increased as dramatically or changed the overall pattern of verified violations as much as the denial of humanitarian access," the study noted.

According to the report, denial of humanitarian access rose from around 2% of all verified grave violations against children in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, becoming the second-most frequently recorded violation after the killing and maiming of children.

Grave violations as laid out in the MRM also include the recruitment of children by armed forces, sexual violence, abduction and attacks on schools and hospitals.

The study found that, overall, 38,967 grave violations against children were verified by the UN.

This was the second-highest annual total since the MRM was established, surpassed only by the record 41,763 violations documented in 2024.

More than half of these took place in just three areas: the Palestinian Territories, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria. The Palestinian Territories alone accounted for 12,449 verified violations, nearly one-third of all cases.

As well as the denial of humanitarian access, violations in 2025 included:.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The Palestinian Territories recorded the highest number of attacks on schools or hospitals, with 837 incidents, followed by Ukraine with 643. Together, the two accounted for more than half of all reported cases worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that the sharpest rises in sexual violence incidents were recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where cases jumped from 358 in 2024 to 592 in 2025, and Sudan, which saw an increase from 74 to 193. Around 86% of all cases were documented in African conflict zones.

"Children have the right to live free from violence. Changing the odds requires political choices that put children’s safety first, and a sustained commitment to stop the war on children," the NGO mentioned.

Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent ⁠protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a latest passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.

To deter ⁠violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson ⁠said.

Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, ​was set on fire late on ‌Wednesday.

It is likely that flammable ‌substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.

According to recent reports, reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.

During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of ‌vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have remarked.

Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police mentioned.

On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops ‌belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.

On Wednesday morning, a bus manufacturer helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses ​were set on fire, authorities remarked.

Industry observers note that tuesday marks a year since Hasina was ​sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.

On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges ⁠over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.

At ​least 37 branches and offices of ​Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or ​attempted fires since 10 November, ‌with 14 more ​attacked since midnight ​on Tuesday, the bank said.

On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.

Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The entire world is now playing Grand Theft Auto VI, with no Newly introduced Zealand trick needed to explore the great fictional state of Leonida.
  • The game sets up the story quickly, but takes its time introducing you to its world.
  • To avoid as many spoilers as possible, I won't talk much about the mission itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The entire world is now playing Grand Theft Auto VI, with no Newly introduced Zealand trick needed to explore the great fictional state of Leonida.

The game sets up the story quickly, but takes its time introducing you to its world. Early in the game, you get to make plenty of choices, but they are often at your own pace. The mission "Hey Arnold" is the first time the game forces you to make an immediate choice whether or not to kill or spare a character called Arnold.

To avoid as many spoilers as possible, I won't talk much about the mission itself. It'll be very clear when you are about to have to make a choice. But players are searching for what to do in this moment. Is Arnold a character that could come back to haunt us? Is he a potential friend who could give us missions down the road?

It has been revealed that the answer is no, Arnold is not a major player in the game. What he represents is a test of Rockstar Games' morality system for the game. Roughly, GTA 6 tracks how aggressive you are, how professional you are, how deadly you are, and how psychopathic you are. So in this moment, you essentially get to decide which kind of person you want your character to be.

Industry observers note that red Dead Redemption 2 had a similar moment during an early train robbery when you could kill or spare the train employees. It felt like a big moment because it carried the emotional weight that only a value system can provide. The characters themselves meant nothing to the plot other than helping shape protagonist Arthur Morgan's nature.

But in all cases, there is no wrong answer, provided you feel your character can look themselves in the mirror afterward. So make your choice and push ahead in your journey in Vice City.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

Eric Miller has more than 20 years of journalism experience, with much of that time spent building and leading teams in the US and UK.

#35727. Hims & Hers launches newly introduced peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1573 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Hims & Hers launches newly introduced peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hims & Hers Health on Wednesday stated it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it announced the upcoming products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • Industry observers note that the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hims & Hers Health on Wednesday stated it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the upcoming products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

Industry observers note that the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October debuted an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson remarked in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

It has been revealed that the company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The tech giant also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The organization remarked it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he stated. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a manufacturer of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

Industry observers note that but health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," stated Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Industry observers note that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

Recent findings suggest that that appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The organization indicates patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

According to recent reports, hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that claims the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "massive fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

Sources indicate that there is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

According to recent reports, glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione showed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also noted in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

Sources indicate that all of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.
  • Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
  • The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, remarked a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he noted. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”.

Recent findings suggest that genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

According to recent reports, the case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later highlighted had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric concerns of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”.

Industry observers note that legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have stated gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

Recent findings suggest that the court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.

Sources indicate that myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

According to recent reports, israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already mentioned Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1099 w)

Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the organization’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.
  • According to recent reports, the announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software.
  • Recent findings suggest that the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the organization’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.

According to recent reports, the announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Consumers will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

Recent findings suggest that the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and newly introduced governance tools arriving alongside them.

It has been revealed that copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been revealed ahead of general availability.

According to recent reports, also revealed as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a organization’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”.

Sources indicate that trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s latest frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he stated.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft claims each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and owners to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure must still be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will need to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Along with the guardrails, Microsoft unveiled what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and MasterCard, to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”.

Sources indicate that along with the other confirmed additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”.

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” stated Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”.

Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for owners across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”.

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure strategy.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that MARSHALL, Mich.
  • Industry observers note that the automaker noted Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.
  • The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

Industry observers note that the automaker noted Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

According to recent reports, the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, mentioned licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as rapidly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to recent reports, in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial aims of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

Breaking: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
  • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
  • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of concerns from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of concerns from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” noted Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

Industry observers note that “Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun remarked. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office confirmed earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

In a recent development, for Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to upcoming heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he mentioned.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

China thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Sources indicate that congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier remarked he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an notable opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government.
  • The Israeli parliament elected a fresh speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
  • The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader presently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government.

The Israeli parliament elected a fresh speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader presently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.

Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.

Sources indicate that he was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.

“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.

The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a newly introduced coalition government.

Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.

As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.

They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.

Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.

“It’s key because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.

Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.

Industry observers note that eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.

Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira stated, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.

Industry observers note that chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.

Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.

“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no latest institution has to be created,” he remarked.

Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.

Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI has only been out for a day, but people are already sharing tips.

One early hidden feature — and a nice way to quickly build those cash reserves — comes courtesy of a liquor store and a talking parrot.

UK streamer Millzaa shared a mini walkthrough of how to find the money in GTA 6 on TikTok and X, where it's been viewed over a million times.

"There's a parrot that leads you to a secret money stash at the start of GTA 6," he says in the video. "Talk to your neighbor Shirley and she'll send you to the liquor store for some rum...".

Millzaa explains that once you've bought and delivered the rum for Shirley you can return to Three Sheets Liquor (when you're in the store earlier, the owner tells a bunch of animals in a back room to be quiet. Don't try to enter this room by walking behind the counter (the owner will not like this). If you jump the fence round the side you'll find some criminals you need to fight off — and when you do, you'll discover a talking red parrot in a cage. The parrot mentions cash and a generator, next to which you'll find a grate in the wall.

Sources indicate that hidden inside? Over $1,300. Nice.

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
  • Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs.
  • Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, Latest Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, Latest Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

In a recent development, two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While replicating the concern in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation.
  • In a recent development, the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical complications behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the concern in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

In a recent development, the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have remarked there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris stated that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

Recent findings suggest that "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators remarked within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.
