⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • Industry observers note that the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

Industry observers note that the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have noted.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it notes is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

It has been revealed that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official remarked in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Industry observers note that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

Recent findings suggest that the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

#35687. Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (923 w)

Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there is always a catch.
  • Industry observers note that last Friday night, Tesla remarked it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs.
  • From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Industry observers note that last Friday night, Tesla remarked it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s “limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

According to recent reports, the business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”.

According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.).

If owners do anything that Tesla deems “unauthorized or inappropriate,” the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.).

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

According to recent reports, for years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers latest services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, Internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a upcoming feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does “ownership” mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for preinstalled hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.

Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the firm has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service presently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

It has been revealed that in exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn’t cover insurance.

It has been revealed that cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly remarked owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence.

Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza.

In the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West. According to a rapid analysis that month by media researchers at the University of Washington, those 400 posts racked up an astonishing 370 million views. As the UW researchers framed it, a 641,000-follower Polish account had just catapulted itself atop a list of “fresh elites” on X, momentarily trouncing the reach of legacy outlets with follower counts in the tens of millions, like CNN, The New York Times, and the BBC.

More to the point, Visegrad had also established itself overnight as one of the most influential pro-Israel accounts on X. And that’s what seemed to be giving Tompson pause.

“With the Israel situation,” Tompson texted his colleague, “I do loathe Hamas, and it’s been the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west” (a long-standing editorial priority for Tompson and his team). But Tompson seemed wary that Israel was already angling for a wider regional conflict. “Personally I want that war to be contained where it is,” Tompson wrote. “And the Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things.”.

It has been revealed that ultimately, the founder reasoned a way through his qualms. In another message from the same day, the cigar-smoking, cravat-wearing, thirtysomething Tompson wrote to the same confidant—whom I’ll call Boris—to spell out how he’d landed with regard to V24’s “editorial line” on Israel. As Tompson saw it, V24 had been faced with “four options” once the war started:.

Industry observers note that 1. Say nothing;2. Be objective—get hated by both sides;3. Pro Muslim—there are 1.5 billion of them;4. Pro Israel—There are fewer but also they have a lot of influence and money.

In choosing between those options, Tompson laid out a blunt motivation: “My goal is to fundraise off of this,” he wrote.

Industry observers note that covering Gaza did fit nicely with V24’s long-standing brand of anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, Western-chauvinist content. (“The beauty of this war is that it allows us to criticize slims—especially those in Europe—without any consequences,” Tompson would later write, using a shorthand slur for Muslims.) But now he seemed to have his eyes on a bigger opportunity: using Visegrad’s “new elite” status to rake in money from some of Israel’s most powerful supporters in Silicon Valley and beyond.

And according to an extensive trove of V24 financial records, internal communications, screenshots from group chats, and correspondence with donors, all reviewed by WIRED, Tompson promptly succeeded at exactly that.

Over the past six years, Visegrad24 has become a strangely ubiquitous force in right-wing social media, its feed a reliable kaleidoscope of dehumanized, brown-skinned aggressors and their alleged depredations against innocent, often white-skinned victims, alongside global news from a nationalist perspective. On any given day, V24 might show you a stomach-turning video of a camel being abused at a wedding in the West Bank, a parade of cell phone clips showing violent crimes being committed by alleged “migrants” all across Europe, or an interview about the Great Replacement Theory.

According to recent reports, from its headquarters in Warsaw, V24’s lean pseudo-news operation has proven itself almost preternaturally adept at virality on Elon Musk’s X. It even seems to have become one of the oligarch’s own favorite accounts. For a period after November 2024, Musk became especially fixated on British far-right politics, posting nonstop about “rape gangs” of South Asian men allegedly grooming British girls. To better understand Musk’s influences at the time, WIRED partnered with the research firm Bright Data to analyze his interactions with some 30 prominent European far-right accounts over a 45-day period ending in January 2025; we found that Musk engaged with Visegrad24, a major font of “grooming gangs” content, at least three times more than any other account on the list. Another dubious mark of distinction for V24: Of all the billion-plus accounts on X, Visegrad ranks 32nd in the number of community notes—crowdsourced fact checks—that have been attached to its posts.

Recent findings suggest that but in tandem with its drumbeat of demonized migrants, V24 has also excelled at capitalizing on the information wars that inevitably form around real, bloody conflicts like those in Ukraine, Gaza, and now Iran. The documents obtained by WIRED—to which Tompson responded with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer—shed an intimate light on how this playbook evolved over the course of V24’s rapid rise. They provide an unvarnished case study of life inside today’s fractured and erratic right-wing mediasphere. And they reveal how the right kind of online influence, even when it’s strategically acquired by an entity just barely above the gutter of white nationalism, can command support from some of the most powerful people in the world.

Sources indicate that in late November 2023, Tompson wrote to Boris with some exciting news. “Jewish VCs have created a group,” he texted. “Several. I’m in two of those groups that actively push back against founders who have supported Palestine.” In another message he described one of these encrypted text threads as “85 people. 84 Jews and me.”.

It has been revealed that “They are slowly reaching out directly … Usually they want a retweet,” he wrote to Boris. “V24 is such a big part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now.”.

“You’re in the belly of the beast now,” replied Boris (who requested anonymity for fear of legal retaliation).

One of the groups to which Tompson gained entry was called Jewish Alliances, described by one of its members—someone going by the handle Sean Rad, which is the name of a Tinder cofounder—as a space to “bring together Jews and non-Jews working together to fight antisemitism.”.

It has been revealed that on Jewish Alliances, Tompson came personally recommended by Shaun Maguire, a general partner at Sequoia Capital who led the firm’s investments in Elon Musk–affiliated companies. Like V24, Maguire had become vociferously pro-Israel after October 7—later explaining that the attacks galvanized him to engage in “information warfare” for the country. Maguire had even made introductions that eventually helped connect the Israel Defense Forces with Musk’s Starlink satellite communication network in the earliest days of the Gaza war. And now, on Jewish Alliances, he was throwing some weight behind V24.

In a recent development, “Stefan / Visegrad is an incredible account if you’re not already following,” Maguire told the group thread. Privately, Maguire told Tompson, “I’ll give u $25k and try to raise the rest.” (Maguire later told WIRED that he ultimately had to stop short of making his donation. “I would have loved to donate to Visegrad, as I think their content is excellent, but I wasn't able to for compliance reasons.”).

As for the other elite group chat that Tompson states he was invited to join, it appears to have been even more rarefied. In December that year, Tompson sent Boris a screenshot of a blurb from a Puck newsletter, headlined “The In-Crowd’s Hottest Text Thread.” Tompson had circled the item in red with an arrow pointing at it.

“I learned this week that hundreds of the most powerful figures from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Hollywood have joined a sprawling, informal WhatsApp thread to share thoughts on how to build support for Israel and combat antisemitism following the attacks of October 7,” wrote media reporter Dylan Byers in the blurb. “The group, which is called Builders for Israel, includes the likes of Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, and David Marcus.”.

“And Stefan Tompson 😂,” Boris replied, to which Tompson responded with his own laughing emoji.

Recent findings suggest that on the two group chats, Tompson sometimes gawked at the proceedings, sending Boris screenshots of what he was witnessing. On November 24, one member posted the following message to the group: “I bought some domains. If anyone would like them to redirect to appropriate content lmk.”.

The member then listed out a series of five urls: “longlivetheintifada.com, wechargeyouwithgenocide.com, palestineisourhome.com, fromtherivertothesee.com, fromtheriver2theseapalestinewillbefree.com.”.

“Btw this is available albeit $75k,” the member went on, before posting a screenshot showing a listing for the domain name “Allahuakbar.com.”.

Tompson himself responded inside the group. “Oh this has so much potential! 💀” he wrote.

(A review of public web domain records indicates that all five of the first urls listed here were registered through GoDaddy using Domains by Proxy, a service that allows domain registrants to hide their personal contact information. The records show that all five were created on November 22, 2023, in two batches 33 minutes apart. It’s unclear whether anyone bought Allahuakbar.com, whose owner is also hidden behind the proxy service, but its registration record was last updated on November 28, 2023.).

As a platform for fundraising, the two group chats appear to have paid off pretty handsomely for Visegrad24. “Should have 75k on Monday,” Tompson wrote to Boris on November 18. There was $50,000 coming from “a very private man” at the Silicon Valley fintech investment firm Ribbit Capital. Ribbit's founder is Meyer “Micky” Malka, an early investor in Coinbase and promoter of crypto. Tompson would later tell Boris that Malka was allegedly planning to donate an additional $200,000. Financial records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 roughly lining up with Tompson's messages, but Malka did not respond to requests for comment. Records indicate that Tompson also secured a $20,000 donation from the investment firm Hindenberg Research, with an additional $15,000 linked to an email address associated with the firm’s founder, the prominent Wall Street short seller Nathan Anderson. Tompson also claimed he had a “soft commitment” from the Israeli American investor Daniel Gross, a former AI lead at both Apple and Y Combinator. (Anderson and Gross did not respond to requests for comment.).

Notifications from GiveButter, a site Tompson used for soliciting contributions, show that other donations were linked to email addresses associated with SimpleVenue CEO Michael Sinensky, Warby Parker founder Neil Blumenthal, Wix president Nir Zohar, Lux Capital cofounder Josh Wolfe, and deep tech venture capitalist Matt Ocko.

(Sinensky and Blumenthal declined to comment, and Zohar’s representatives remarked they had no record of him donating. Wolfe and Ocko neither confirmed nor denied that they’d given money to V24, but both came back with remarkably similar responses, primarily taking glitch with WIRED’s characterization of whether Visegrad is “far right.” “I don't fund or support ‘far right’ groups,” Wolfe wrote, “and thankfully Stefan and Visegard24 are pro-democracy, pro-Western values, pro-peace and prosperity.” Wrote Ocko: “Even cursory research indicates that neither Mr. Tompson, nor Visegrad24 are affiliated with or support anything other than: classical liberal Western values, including the rule of law; the defense of democratic polities from terror and autocracies … peace and prosperity for all law-abiding and civilized people; opposition to horrific antisemitism and terrorist exaltation.”).

While Tompson was fundraising away with his group-chat contacts, Boris wrote with a question. “By the way, should I take Middle Eastern money?” he asked, mentioning opportunities to raise funds from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Sources indicate that “100 percent yes. Play both sides,” Tompson said. “I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs.”.

According to recent reports, to receive its donations, V24 set up an organization under the 501(c)(3) umbrella called the Intermarium Foundation, headquartered in Pennsylvania but domiciled in Delaware. Over the next year and more, over a million dollars poured in. Much of the money, including some of the largest sums, appears to have come in through “donor advised funds”—“dark money” philanthropic vehicles that allow donors to hide their identities, even from the recipients of their cash. Foundation documents show that in November 2024, the organization received $175,000 from DonorsTrust, a fund closely aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, often referred to as the “dark money ATM” of the American right. Documents also suggest that V24 received $172,000 from the Giving Back Fund, which describes itself as a “national nonprofit organization that encourages and facilitates charitable giving by professional athletes, celebrities, high-net-worth individuals, existing nonprofit organizations, corporations, and others.”.

Sources indicate that A London-born self-described “Polish South African” who was “educated in French schools,” Tompson founded Visegrad24 in early 2020. He'd moved to Warsaw from London in the mid-2010s, having worked as a PR strategist on the “Leave” side of the Brexit campaign, according to Gizmodo. Tompson’s great-grandfather, he has remarked, was the Polish ambassador to England at the time of the Nazi invasion. Between the war and the communist takeover of Poland, the family was left stranded abroad for three generations. In a 2024 interview with Jewish Insider, Tompson referred to his arrival in Warsaw as his “own version of aliyah,” the Hebrew word used to describe a Jewish person’s immigration to Israel.

Tompson’s homecoming took place just as Poland was attempting to aggressively pattern itself after Viktor Orban’s Hungary. In 2015, the illiberal, nationalist Law and Justice Party swept Polish elections and set about packing courts, hollowing institutions, and seizing control of Polish state radio, newspapers, and television—turning the latter into nakedly xenophobic, anti-opposition, and often antisemitic propaganda organs.

With his taste for cravats and posh Barbour jackets, Tompson found an audience on Polish state TV documentaries extolling the country’s grand cultural heritage. He started a PR agency called Bracia Tompson SC, and according to the investigative site VSquare, he made short films with the support of something called the Institute for the Legacy of Polish National Thought, described by the Polish news outlet Polytka as a slush fund for the governing party.

Tompson also spent the late 2010s working on what he described as a “three-hour documentary” about his father’s ancestral home, South Africa—a country whose quality of life, Tompson claimed in a 2019 Polish radio interview, is worse today than under apartheid. The documentary project was reportedly titled African Volhynia, after an area in Central Europe where Poles suffered historic massacres, land dispossession, and ethnic cleansing—a framing that, to some observers, strongly suggests that Tompson was packaging a South African “white genocide” narrative for a Polish audience. The full documentary, however, was never released.

Sources indicate that instead, Tompson shifted focus to launch Visegrad24 in January 2020, with a logo closely mirroring the South African outlet News24. The name Visegrad is a reference to the Visegrad Group, an informal diplomatic bloc of four Central European nations that includes Poland and Hungary. In 2020, it was Poland’s turn to occupy the rotating presidency of the alliance—and V24 appears to have served a promotional function. When V24’s Facebook page was briefly blocked for violating community standards in 2021, the Polish deputy minister of foreign affairs spoke up for the account. “The Visegrad24 profile is not an official profile of the Visegrad Group or the Polish presidency of the Visegrad Group,” he told a Polish radio station. “However, we appreciate it for its promotion of the group’s activities.”.

According to recent reports, one of Tompson’s main partners in the enterprise was a Polish journalist named Adam Starzynski, the former proprietor of an ultra-right-wing Twitter account called @BasedPoland and reportedly a fellow board member at something called the State of Poland Foundation. Their third, more silent founder was Tompson’s brother Jan. Tompson’s sister Alexandra also became involved, sometimes serving as a de facto legal rep.

In its early years, Visegrad24 posted roughly in line with the Law and Justice Party’s priorities—positively about Poland’s abortion ban, negatively about migrants, fulsomely about Christianity and Hungarian fertility rates—and was tagged frequently by party officials, according to Polish investigative site OKO.Press.

In a recent development, but Tompson harbored bigger ambitions, as well as some apparent personal struggles. In early 2022, Visegrad’s core team escaped the Polish winter by renting a house together in the Canary Islands—during which time Tompson was said to be “undergoing acute drug withdrawal and was in a very vulnerable state,” according to an email later written by Alexandra and reviewed by WIRED. (In a couple of messages, Tompson refers to a time in his life when he was “on coke.”).

The team had been in Gran Canaria for about a month when something momentous happened: Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. In the early morning hours of February 24, they woke up to images of Russian tanks crossing Ukraine’s borders. They immediately began pushing out an intense volume of news and clickbait.

Sources indicate that bit by bit, Visegrad started gaining international traction—and international notoriety for spreading fake news. On February 25, Visegrad tweeted “PornHub cockblocks Russian people,” alleging that Russian porn seekers “were presented with a message saying the content is blocked along with a Ukrainian flag and a message of support to Ukraine”—a rumor that was debunked by Snopes and other online fact-checkers. Then, about a week later, V24 tweeted that actor Leonardo DiCaprio had donated $10 million to Ukraine in honor of his grandmother from Odesa. (DiCaprio made no such donation, and there is no evidence of such a grandmother.) Articles debunking V24’s claim promptly appeared on Snopes and CNN.

According to recent reports, this first brush with global virality came with risks. Elon Musk didn’t own Twitter yet, and content moderation was strict. “I’m really stressing out over v24,” Tompson wrote in an internal WhatsApp group named Gran Canaria. But rather than get shut down, V24 lived to see its follower count triple, growing from 80,000 to 250,000 in weeks.

Sources indicate that V24’s boosted reach didn’t bring an end to Tompson’s frustrations, however. He appeared dissatisfied with the liberal followers that came along with being such a prominent pro-Ukrainian account. And he also seemed to be running into patronage problems: In 2022, the Polish news outlet Wiadomości revealed that the office of Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had tried to allocate about $300,000 for “the implementation of the public project titled ‘Visegrad24,’” sending money to a sports and fitness NGO called the Action-Life Foundation. Then, in 2023, according to OKO.press, Morawiecki’s office appears to have sent a bit under $600,000 for a “media center” at the Action-Life Foundation—which appeared, yet again, to be a carve-out for a V24-affiliated project. This time the grant was recalled after public outcry. (In an interview, Tompson has said he “never had a penny to run Visegrad” from the Polish state.) In October 2023, the Law & Justice Party lost its majority in parliament, ending eight years of right-wing dominance over Polish government purse strings.

By that fall, Tompson seems to have realized that V24’s Canary Islands posting blitz had yielded a huge bump in influence that they’d failed to monetize. In terms of fundraising, Tompson told Boris, “we missed the boat with Ukraine.” So when V24 repeated its flood-the-zone strategy with the October 7 attacks, Tompson seemed determined not to skip the next step.

It has been revealed that by early 2024, Tompson was sitting down in Tel Aviv for a podcast interview with the American-born Israeli venture capitalist Michael Eisenberg—often billed as an informal adviser to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Less than six months had passed since October 7, and Tompson was on his way to becoming a minor celebrity among friends of Israel. “Meet the Man Who Shapes Millions of Twitter Owners’ view of Israel’s war,” ran the headline of a story in the Jewish Chronicle, which went on to describe a series of V24 videos Tompson’s team had been filming on the streets of the West Bank. “Anyone who states it is an apartheid state in Israel and the Palestinian people are subjugated should go to Ramallah,” Tompson told the news outlet. “There were Maseratis and Mercedes and a brand-upcoming shopping mall.” As of that month, at least 28,473 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since October 7, and at least 388 had been killed in the West Bank, Israel, and East Jerusalem, according to the United Nations.

Tompson was also busily fundraising. “The west is under attack,” claimed a sleek V24 donor pitch deck dated August 2024 and later reviewed by WIRED. “We face two major adversaries: radical progressives” and “nefarious States (Russia, Iran, China, Qatar).” The pitch deck called V24 “the frontier of modern journalism for western values.”.

It has been revealed that one pitch deck promoted “Project Q,” a social media campaign against Qatar. In a single month, Project Q had delivered “97 posts about Qatar across multiple accounts,” 12 original pieces of video content, including a “viral” short featuring the British anti-Islamic activist Tommy Robinson, video essays, and an instance of then Polish MEP Michał Dworczyk condemning Qatar in a speech.

V24 also boasted that it was building “a network of Muslim and Arab influencers to push content,” including pro-Israel voices Loay Alshareef, Nuseir Yassin, Luai Ahmed, and YouTuber “Apostate Prophet,” the latter an ex-Muslim interviewee on V24’s YouTube.

It has been revealed that then there was the Project Veritas–style hidden-camera news operation Tompson had launched, called V24 Investigations, run by the ex-Project Veritas board member Matthew Tyrmand. In the spring of 2024, V24 Investigations fanned out across American university campuses amid pro-Palestine protests to make unflattering, Project Veritas–style videos of student activists, part of a larger V24 effort to expand its YouTube presence.

But in 2025 and 2026, Visegrad would see more opportunity to draw on a traditional area of strength—breaking war news on X.

In a recent development, on June 13, 2025, Israel leaped into the wider conflict that Tompson had initially been afraid of: That morning, Tel Aviv brutally ambushed Iran with an onslaught of synchronized assassinations, air raids, and drone strikes—and V24 aggressively posted through it on X. But this time, alongside its fairly typical mix of war porn and mockery of pro-Palestinian protesters, a somewhat unusual motif ran through Visegrad’s social coverage of the war: Enthusiasm for restoring the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah.

According to recent reports, V24 even played a bit part in the social media war to influence US president Donald Trump as he toyed with joining Israel’s fight. On the fifth day of the war—after Trump had stated on Truth Social, “We know exactly where the so-called ‘Supreme Leader’ is hiding”—Visegrad chimed in with a post on X seemingly tailor-made to sweeten the option of regime change:.

Incoming reports of Iranian military officers seeking contact with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi to declare their intent to defect. They also want to pledge their allegiance to His Majesty and his mission to lead the transition to democracy in Iran after the regime’s fall.

Visegrad’s post received more than a million views and was shared nearly 3,000 times.

When Trump finally did make his move four days later, dropping a set of “bunker buster” bombs on Iranian nuclear sites, V24 posted an image of the Islamic Republic’s flag being torn away to reveal that of the Pahlavi monarchy and the words “It’s time” (2.4 million views, 3,600 shares).

Why the outsize focus on the sexagenarian exiled son of a former dictator? Pahlavi does enjoy a certain amount of organic political support among the Iranian diaspora. But he’s also been held up at times as Israel’s preferred leader for Iran. In October 2025, Haaretz, TheMarker, and the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab reported that Israel’s government was likely behind a massive Persian-language “influence operation” to simulate online support for Pahlavi using bots, synchronized posting campaigns, and artificial intelligence—all “as part of an even broader Israeli campaign to influence the social media discourse.”.

Recent findings suggest that V24’s own pro-Pahlavi posting binge was underway at the same time. When asked whether V24 had received any funding from Pahlavi’s network, Tompson responded by saying, “I wasn’t aware that Reza Pahlavi was a foreign state.” When asked whether he had received any money from Israel directly, Tompson replied with an apparent joke. “Yes,” he wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu personally hands me money for every post on Visegrad24.”.

In the three years since October 7, Visegrad24’s follower count has swelled to 2.1 million on X. But even as Musk’s platform has stubbornly remained V24’s only real area of strength, it has also become a more contested one since 2023. “They’re operating in an extremely competitive space,” claims Ryan Broderick, the founder of the Garbage Day newsletter, which tracks the online media ecosystem.

According to recent reports, in recent years, with the rise of open-source-intelligence “monitoring the situation” accounts on X—essentially breaking-news channels run by hyper-online finance people—real-time coverage of crises and conflicts has become more of a crowded market, states Broderick. Today, he figures, an October 7–style V24 posting blitz would have a harder time breaking through. At the same time, V24’s other stock and trade—xenophobic posts about migrants—is easily upstaged by countless accounts that are more nakedly, brazenly racist.

Meanwhile, support for Israel has only become a more isolating position to occupy on the global far right, which has leaned further and further into its natural affinity for noxious antisemitism. (In 2025, Tompson appears to have met up in Turkey with another right-wing video creator named Lord Miles—a British self-styled adventurer who denigrates many of the same ethnic groups that V24 does, only with the addition of being blatantly antisemitic. According to Lord Miles, the two were set to collaborate on a video. But then Tompson started talking about raising six-figure sums from a pro-Israel “WhatsApp group chat,” and Lord Miles bolted from the scene, later posting about the episode on X.).

It has been revealed that relatively early in its reporting on V24, WIRED reached out to some people who know Tompson, including an ex-partner. Shortly afterward, Tompson called back from her phone. “That’s not how we do things in South Africa, my friend,” he said. “I don’t like it. I find it creepy; I find it weird.” He then offered to pay for a flight to Warsaw for an on-the-record interview with him—an offer WIRED declined, given journalistic standards against accepting money from sources. “Are you not a man, my friend?” Tompson said. “I’m very upset you have disrespected me.”.

Industry observers note that when WIRED later got in touch to arrange a concrete date for a phone interview, Tompson asked if he could be sent questions in advance. When WIRED refused, citing standard editorial practice, Tompson balked. “Not really interested in you wasting my time old sport,” he wrote, “What exactly is the incentive for me to give you any more of my time, generosity or politeness?” He signed off the message with the words, “praying that you find Christ, who redeems all, including the likes of sinning wretches like myself.”.

Industry observers note that he later turned WIRED’s reporter’s request for an interview around. “Now I am kindly offering you the opportunity to answer some questions,” he wrote. “It’s a generous offer, which will allow you to give your perspective on things and answer some notable questions about your behavior, your lifestyle, your funding, and some other details that are an important reflection of you who are as a person.” WIRED declined.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu.

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.

An Israeli military spokesperson stated troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military remarked it had been “completed”.

The IDF ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.

It has been revealed that residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics stated one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

After the statement from the IDF that it had concluded the tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, the defence ministry’s body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Cogat, mentioned Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics remarked two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.

In a recent development, israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it notes has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.

Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.

Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace stated the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel rolled out its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. A previous report by the commission in September 2025 found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited those acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • Recent findings suggest that sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Recent findings suggest that sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this newly introduced material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

In a recent development, we’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the organization when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Sources indicate that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced looks for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The tech giant opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, notes Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky claims, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

In a recent development, the glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sources indicate that sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he mentioned. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our manufacturer. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

In a recent development, autosaving in games has spoiled us all. We've become complacent. We used to actively save games like our lives (or Banjo and Kazooie's lives) depended on it.

It has been revealed that but saving in Grand Theft Auto VI is absolutely crucial if you're the type of person who regrets choices immediately or wants to follow different paths with myriad saves. You didn't want to kill that guy or trespass on that lawn? Everyone's mad at you, the police are in hot pursuit, but the last time the game saved was an hour ago? I feel that.

Industry observers note that the question is: can you manually save in GTA 6? In short: if you're on a mission, no; if you're not, yes.

As in most games, you can manually save GTA 6 in the open world sections between missions. Just hit the pause button, open up the options menu, hit save, and pick a slot. Here, you can enter multiple saves in case you want to see how a storyline with a major choice pans out multiple ways.

But you must save before starting a mission if you're looking to explore a sliding doors moment. During missions in GTA 6, you can't save the game.

Recent findings suggest that when Radio Times asked GTA 6 game system design director Ben Rollinson why they made it impossible to save during missions, he told the outlet, "It was on the cards for a while, but there was a concern with issues around maintaining and testing loading fresh into every checkpoint of every mission on top of all the other game states that we save. We ultimately decided to optimize how saves were supported to ensure the experience was clean throughout the full game.".

If you want to change your actions during a mission, you'll have to do the whole thing again by loading a previous save or by selecting to restart the mission or last checkpoint. So, make sure you're manually saving GTA 6 as you go, or at least right before missions.

Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators.
  • The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has noted.
  • The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators.

The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has noted.

The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.

Lynch, 59, had been enjoying a voyage around Sicily with family and friends after his acquittal in a long-running fraud case regarding the sale of the technology firm he founded, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard in 2011.

He and his 18-year-old daughter, Hannah, died, as did lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife, Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife, Judy, and the yacht’s chef, Recaldo Thomas. Nine other crew members and six guests were rescued.

The MAIB final report, published on Thursday, appears to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecutors have reportedly blamed errors by the crew.

It has been revealed that the MAIB report details how the yacht was hit “by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast” of about 70 knots (80 mph), which knocked it on to its side in less than 15 seconds. It sank 18 minutes later.

Investigators found that the yacht’s vulnerability to strong winds had never been assessed for the conditions in which it was anchored, with its sails down and its retractable centreboard raised. The centreboard is a large underwater structure that helps a sailing vessel remain stable.

The extreme weather was most likely caused by a downburst – a powerful blast of air from a thunderstorm that hits the sea and spreads out with enormous force, the report remarked.

None of the life rafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel. The crew managed to release one manually. Survivors were rescued by crew from a nearby yacht, the Sir Robert Baden-Powell.

Recent findings suggest that rob Loder, the chief inspector of MAIB, mentioned: “This accident developed with extraordinary speed. In just 14 minutes, calm conditions had given way to winds of at least 68 knots, which in less than 15 seconds pushed the yacht on to its side.

“Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down. The extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk.”.

Industry observers note that the report conveys the desperate minutes as the Bayesian was knocked down. Crew were alerted by sudden and severe winds of up to 30 knots at 03.55, and within two minutes the yacht listed starboard and the vessel began to drag anchor before the wind suddenly increased to about 70 knots.

“At 04.06 Bayesian violently heeled over 90 degrees to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on,” the report said.

Some guests, awoken by the listing and who had left their cabins, escaped. One couple used furniture drawers as an improvised ladder. Guests who managed to get to the flying bridge were instructed to swim away from the vessel and warned to stay clear of the mast and boom as it sank.

It has been revealed that passengers and crew who made it out gathered in the water, using a torch on a mobile to search for others. A crew member managed to swim back to the yacht to manually release one life raft from stowage. By 04.24 the life raft was inflated.

It has been revealed that the investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.

It noted information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast also did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms it predicted, it said.

Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking at the deaths of Mike and Hannah Lynch and Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, who were all British nationals.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Indian woman lights lamps on the occasion of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights.
  • India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
  • A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Indian woman lights lamps on the occasion of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights.

India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.

A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.

The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.

The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.

Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.

The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.

Muslims offer prayer at the historic Jama Masjid in Delhi.

It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.

The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.

Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.

If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.

According to recent reports, despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.

Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.

Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.

"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.

Hindu devotees offer prayers on the banks of the Sabarmati river in India's Gujarat.

"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably â from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she mentioned.

"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.).

The projections are hardly surprising, claims KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.

Recent findings suggest that "The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.

"Ultimately, they will converge," he notes, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.

In a recent development, demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".

Muslim children dressed in festive attire in India.

The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.

Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.

There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.

Industry observers note that by 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.

In a recent development, christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.

But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.

Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.

Recent findings suggest that the report states that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.

With more than 1.4 billion people, India overtook China in 2023 in terms of population, according to the UN.

Sources indicate that the steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report indicates.

The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.

One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.

In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.

Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.

Recent findings suggest that china accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.

By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.

The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.

And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.

Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.

Muslims offer Eid prayers in Pakistan.

According to recent reports, there are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.

"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.

India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed.

Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.

South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.

Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

#35673. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he notes.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Industry observers note that pulitano states the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Industry observers note that perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, claims about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

In a recent development, scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, claims Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano claims his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

In a recent development, what’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, upcoming types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

Sources indicate that for his part, Pulitano claims long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s notable to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

Sources indicate that he’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has mentioned it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, notes Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two fresh scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

Recent findings suggest that “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” notes Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waymo is presently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars’ driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.”.

In a recent development, this is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations.

In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”.

Waymo also told the government that the updated software is better able to respond to emergency vehicles when in a construction zone and that the company has made “operational changes that better identify and mitigate potential entry into pre-planned construction zones and enable more Remote Assistance capability” if it happens again.

Which it has. Despite the update to improve behavior around emergency vehicles, a video went viral in early November showing a Waymo robotaxi on I-280 driving past a pair of California Highway Patrol cars conducting a rolling roadblock as they held traffic behind a slow-moving construction vehicle. California also indicates there was an incident in which a Waymo robotaxi entered a construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Waymo told Ars. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

Waymo also told Ars it was continuing to work with the various California agencies that regulate transport.

Until the suspension, Waymo was only conducting highway operations in Los Angeles and the Bay Area in California, as well as in Arizona.

Breaking: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
