📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.
  • According to recent reports, "GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records.
  • Industry observers note that A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.

According to recent reports, "GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.

Industry observers note that A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.

As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.

To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.

According to recent reports, expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).

"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," notes Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.

It has been revealed that when such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.

In a recent development, this video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.

The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.

In a recent development, what makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.

"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.

Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.

At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.

The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.

But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.

Industry observers note that former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health problems. Trade unions accuse organization managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.

Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.

Assessment of damage under way, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia.

The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, leading to a halt in train services, two days after a dramatic Ukrainian air raid had knocked out the road bridge alongside.

Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, noted on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.

It has been revealed that emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.

The latest air raid took place hours before the unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between Donald Trump, the US president, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, his Russian and Chinese counterparts.

It has been revealed that it was the third time that the $3.6bn bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, has been struck in a week. On Tuesday, a 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed after a complex missile and drone attack that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.

Ukrainian military sources had indicated the timing of the attack on the road bridge was deliberate, ahead of the summit, suggesting that the follow-up raid on the rail bridge overnight may have been intended to bring it down as well.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces remarked this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

It has been revealed that for Ukraine, the bridge across the Kerch strait is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation. A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.

Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.

According to recent reports, flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central road section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch. A range of weapons, including Ukraine’s Neputune cruise missile and the Ruta, made by Dutch tech giant Destinus, targeted the adjacent rail section, Zelenskyy stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic.

In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The manufacturer behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it mentioned on Wednesday.

At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (Â£14.7bn) each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it rolled out Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Industry observers note that initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the manufacturer were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile.

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she states, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their newly introduced venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Sources indicate that now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the Latest York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sources indicate that sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the manufacturer after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the manufacturer's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Danish foreign minister states deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding.
  • The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a fresh Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory.
  • The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danish foreign minister states deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding.

The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a fresh Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory.

The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system.

It also recognises Greenland, a former Danish colony, as an equal partner and stipulates that if it were to become fully independent of Denmark, it would remain in Nato.

Having already been approved by the Greenlandic parliament earlier this month, all that remained for the agreement to come into effect, said the Danish foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, was for Trump to send a notification to the US Congress.

In a recent development, “We have now resolved our part of the equation,” Løkke Rasmussen remarked after the bill was passed. “This is a positive development, as it removes all uncertainty surrounding Greenland and establishes a proper framework for future cooperation.”.

But he warned that trust with the US had been damaged. “Consequently, there is a significant task of rebuilding ahead. But this will take place within the framework of an agreement, which is a good thing,” he noted.

Before the deal was signed, Trump said the US would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland”. But Løkke Rasmussen said on Thursday that the US was yet to inform Denmark of any prepares to establish fresh military bases.

The US ambassador to Denmark, Ken Howery, said on social media he was “thrilled that the Danish parliament today voted unanimously 109-0 to ratify the Greenland security agreement”.

In a statement, he said: “On behalf of the United States, I welcome the strong support in Denmark’s parliament for the ratification of the historic US-Denmark-Greenland defence agreement, paving the way for it to enter into force.

“The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernises our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of Nato.”.

He added: “Thank you to colleagues in Denmark and Greenland for the many hours spent negotiating the agreement, which makes us safer, stronger and more secure. I look forward to continuing our work to deepen our cooperation as we implement the agreement and advance other shared priorities with our friends and allies throughout the kingdom of Denmark.”.

Relations between the US and Denmark and Greenland – and the Nato alliance as a whole – had come under unprecedented strain amid repeated threats by Trump to take over the Arctic territory that led to Denmark preparing for a US invasion.

Such was the perceived threat in January that Copenhagen reportedly sent over blood bags, and explosives to blow up runways, in case of US attack.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
  • Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
  • But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

Industry observers note that so she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer.".

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival â Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (Â£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your manufacturer be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

Industry observers note that the company is selling roughly $81bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

âDaniela Amodei: The price of AIâ.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she notes, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider.".

Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI.

What a firm is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future customers of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at Upcoming York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices.".

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

According to recent reports, but these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.

It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

Sources indicate that there is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to substantial tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang and another with a organization executive who reported to him.

Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a newly introduced champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic â and its CEO are to be AI's latest Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.

Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.

He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of fresh more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it â the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development â means that buying interest is high.

It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.

With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.

Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are right now back to $145.

The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.

Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

Recent findings suggest that "Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again.".

It has been revealed that fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she claims.

"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade.".

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

The Las Vegas Grand Prix is always a special experience, but Lego is adding some brick-built magic this year.

Lego and Formula 1 have declared the next phase of their partnership: a 2027 Lego Speed Champions Formula 1 collection featuring brick-built replicas of all 11 team cars and 22 official F1 drivers recreated as Lego minifigures.

In a recent development, the full collection hits shelves globally on March 1, 2027, with preorders live from Nov. 19 in select regions.

In a recent development, to celebrate the launch, Lego is staging its inaugural Lego Race on the Las Vegas Strip circuit on Nov. 21, putting a mystery lineup of drivers behind the wheel of life-size, drivable 28,000-brick F1 minicars ahead of the main Grand Prix. The Lego Races were absolutely wild in Miami and Silverstone. Here's hoping for more of the same in Vegas.

According to recent reports, the biggest pull of this new launch is the minifigures. Previously, Lego's F1 Speed Champions collections nailed the cars, but the cockpits were always staffed by unnamed helmeted drivers. Turning the actual grid into collectible minifigures fixes the single biggest complaint from F1 fans and collectors.

Industry observers note that while preorders are open in select regions, none of these sets will arrive in time for the 2026 holiday gifting window — the collection doesn't officially launch until March 1, 2027. That's a tough wait, but at least we can all check out this weekend's Lego Race before the Las Vegas GP.

  • The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.

“ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.”.

The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.

This represents an key revelation from ULA and will provide some major relief to different parts of the US aerospace community, particularly Blue Origin and NASA.

Recent findings suggest that that’s because the BE-4 engine is also the bedrock of Blue Origin’s Latest Glenn rocket. This powerful rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that was later attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.

After this anomaly, Blue Origin retrofitted the main oxygen valve, including for Vulcan missions. Now it’s clear that this retrofit was not implicated in the Vulcan accident. With the preliminary Vulcan investigation having largely exonerated the BE-4 engine, Blue Origin can press ahead with its return-to-flight mission with Newly introduced Glenn, which could occur as soon as January.

“Following the Vulcan anomaly, Blue Origin immediately worked alongside ULA to review flight data and support the investigation,” Blue Origin said in a statement Wednesday. “Together, we identified that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines. ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”.

Amid a worsening US launch crunch, Upcoming Glenn offers the most tangible option for near-term relief for satellite operators, including Amazon Leo, which lost dozens of satellites on Sunday. The heavy-lift rocket has many commercial and government customers lined up for launch. NASA in particular is counting on the rocket to launch a number of lunar missions in the next two years, as well as play a significant role in landing humans on the Moon later this decade.

It has been revealed that also a relief to NASA will be confirmation that Vulcan’s upper stage, the Centaur V, did not contribute to the failure. NASA recently contracted with ULA to use the Centaur V as its new upper stage for the Space Launch System rocket, enabling future missions to the Moon.

For ULA, however, the latest update only brings more challenges.

Sources indicate that vulcan represents the company’s great hope to remain relevant in a US launch industry increasingly dominated by SpaceX and newer entrants such as Blue Origin. With Vulcan on the sidelines, other companies, such as Relativity Space, Rocket Lab, and Stoke Space, could also elbow out the once all-powerful launch firm.

Industry observers note that although Sunday’s Vulcan flight, its fifth overall, was the first outright mission failure for the rocket, two previous introduces also experienced problems. Those complications involved the nozzle of the solid rocket boosters. ULA has now spent three years trying to move the rocket out of its teething phase and into regular operations. A successful launch on Sunday could have set up at least a monthly launch cadence next year.

According to recent reports, now, the cash-strapped organization must also contend with a new issue involving propellant management and complicated plumbing that feeds liquid oxygen and methane to the BE-4 engines. It will certainly be offline for several months.

What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility.
  • The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
  • It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility.

UK politics live – latest updates.

The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.

The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.

First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.

According to recent reports, A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.

The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-30 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.

With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two significant issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.

To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must come into force together.

Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe initiative, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a major priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.

The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.

It has been revealed that the EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.

In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.

Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.

The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.

Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027; the current arrangement applies only for the 2027-8 academic year.

It has been revealed that in a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety, and examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.

According to recent reports, far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.

Sources indicate that burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he mentioned on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.

The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.

In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DJ Lag is one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers.

South African DJ Lag notes it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.

DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers, is among several African stars to feature, alongside Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake.

"I can't explain the feeling. I started playing the game last night and it's amazing," DJ Lag told the BBC's Newsday programme, adding that he had been playing GTA since he was about 10 years old and could hardly believe he was now part of the latest edition.

Many players have already had a chance to play the game following its worldwide launch.

The game, which lets players explore a fictional American city, features a dedicated African music radio station playing Afrobeats, amapiano and other sounds from across the continent.

The release of GTA 6 ends a 13-year wait for a upcoming edition of the game.

GTA 6 is a satirical video series associated with crime and violence.

Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.

Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.

Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.

DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.

He posted on Instagram: "God did.".

Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.

Rockstar has also confirmed a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.

For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.

The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.

The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.

Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.

The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.

Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.

The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.

The fresh release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi chaired a meeting of the Union Council of Ministers at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Wednesday, hours after returning from the Philippines.

"Council of ministers meeting since morning, extensive discussions on good governance initiatives," he wrote on social media.

Eleven secretaries, including those from the Home and Finance ministries, made presentations, according to local media. Topics included a recent World Bank report on India's progress in reducing extreme poverty, governance reforms, and welfare and youth schemes.

Modi sought feedback on targets set at the ministers' September "chintan shivir," or "brainstorming camp," where ministries were told to ensure 100% saturation of welfare schemes, Business Standard reported.

The meeting lasted about three and a half hours.

Industry observers note that henry Nicholls made an unbeaten 113 to help New Zealand recover from 70-5 to finish the first day of the first Test at 243-5 in Wellington on Thursday. India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and chose to bowl.

Jasprit Bumrah, playing his first Test in about a year, bowled Latest Zealand captain Tom Latham with the third ball of the match. He finished with 3-52 from 17 overs, adding Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell.

Sources indicate that nicholls and Glenn Phillips then added an unbroken 173 after lunch as the pitch eased and India's other pacers lost their lines. Nicholls' 12th Test hundred came from 188 balls, 141 of them dot balls.

Sources indicate that devdutt Padikkal dropped him on 102. Phillips was 94 not out.

"You play at a venue like this and against a team like India, it's a special occasion," AFP cited Nicholls as saying.

India's batting coach, Sitanshu Kotak, remarked the team's less experienced bowlers could learn from how Bumrah adjusted to Upcoming Zealand conditions, AFP reported.

Parts of Bangladesh shut down Thursday as police reported two members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed and the ancestral home of former interim leader Muhammad Yunus was set on fire.

The unrest comes ahead of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile in India next month, despite facing the death sentence there.

Her party, the Awami League, which was banned after Hasina was ousted, called for the nationwide "lockdown" after a week of protests over the government's rejection of her request for a fresh passport and identity card.

Police remarked two local BNP leaders were killed in Narail when Awami League activists attacked a BNP march, local media reported. It added that two other people, a local BNP leader and a transport worker, died in Faridpur and Pirojpur earlier this week.

Newspaper reports remarked suspected BNP activists attacked or set fire to the homes of two Awami League leaders in Dhaka.

Crude bombs went off in Dhaka before dawn and at least four people were wounded, the Press Trust of India reported. Reuters said 97 platoons of the Border Guard had been deployed across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur.

Sources indicate that authorities noted flammable material was probably thrown into an unused ground-floor room of Yunus's Chattogram family home, and that relatives living upstairs were safe. At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices, which Yunus founded, have been targeted since November 10, the bank said.

According to recent reports, home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said those behind the violence will be identified and prosecuted, and he accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting it. Awami League leaders could not be reached for comment, Reuters said.

Odisha has evacuated tens of thousands of people ahead of Cyclone Akvan, which is expected to cross the coast by noon Friday, the third severe cyclonic storm to threaten India's east coast in less than a month.

Industry observers note that the India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha with winds up to 110 kmph. The IMD now expects a severe cyclonic storm, not the very severe storm it projected earlier. Local media reported red alerts for heavy to extremely heavy rain in both states.

In a recent development, reuters cited the chief minister's office, which stated more than 47,000 people had been evacuated by Thursday. Local media put the figure at about 50,000 and said 3,000 cyclone shelters had been opened.

Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi remarked most evacuees were from Ganjam district. Schools in Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal are shut for three days from Thursday. Later, authorities announced that schools in Malkangiri, Rayagada and Koraput districts would also remain closed on Thursday and Friday.

It has been revealed that "No evacuations in Andhra Pradesh yet," state disaster official Prakhar Jain told Reuters. "The storm has reduced in intensity.".

Cyclone Arnab struck the region in late October and Cyclone Murasu earlier this month.

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit.
  • Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
  • For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit.

Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Recent findings suggest that ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines.

First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.

However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fifth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.

Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.

Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.

Sources indicate that the US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.

Trump would like China to be included in any latest agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

In a recent development, xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025.

This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.

Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.

Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.

But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.

Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.

There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.

Industry observers note that of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.

The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.

So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.

For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.

But the power it projects is vital for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy.

He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

According to recent reports, xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

Sources indicate that at a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a upcoming era.

Latest Update: YouTube will start boosting public view counts when you watch on a TV

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It will estimate co-views based on a ‘privacy-safe statistical model.’.
  • YouTube view counts are about to go up (again) thanks to a new metric.
  • YouTube thinks that is has been undercounting viewers in group-watching situations, thus not giving creators a true picture of a video's reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It will estimate co-views based on a ‘privacy-safe statistical model.’.

YouTube view counts are about to go up (again) thanks to a new metric. Google's video streaming platform may count more than one person when videos are viewed on a TV, according to an X post from YouTube Creator Insider. These extra "co-views" will apply to long form, Shorts, and Live videos, for TV views only.

YouTube thinks that is has been undercounting viewers in group-watching situations, thus not giving creators a true picture of a video's reach. The goal with the new metric, the platform wrote, is to "[align] with TV industry standards — including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.".

How, you might wonder, will YouTube know who else is watching besides the account-holder? The platform emphasized that it won't use "devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that." Rather, views will be estimated using a "privacy-safe statistical mode" based on things like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against real-life testing data. YouTube didn't share any other methodology details.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced system will show higher public view counts and watch times for videos, giving creators more data to guide their channel strategy, brand pitches and more (the co-view parameter won't be retroactively applied). What it won't get them is more ad money. "Co-views don't impact ad revenue or YPP thresholds," YouTube Creator Insider wrote. "Creator earnings, AdSense payouts and YouTube Partner Program eligibility remain based on Qualified Views and Watch Hours.".

It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill?
  • These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.
  • But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?”.

These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.

But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn’t experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized’s 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home.

It has been revealed that given my preference for biking over driving, I need a bike that can get me across town at a decent clip without draining an entire charge. That’s exactly what the Evo delivered on my longest rides.

Industry observers note that what sold me on the bike was a 24-mile round trip that took 83 minutes and used just 56 percent of the battery. According to Specialized’s app, which connects to the bike over Bluetooth, I averaged 235 W of assist power while moving an average of 17 mph, though I was generally closer to 20 mph on stretches where I didn’t have to slow down. I also hit a max speed of 27.3 mph with little effort.

Industry observers note that the bike is a beast, weighing around 70 pounds for the large-size frame I tested. Despite being the heaviest e-bike I’ve ridden, the Evo makes pedaling easier than ever. The bike lacks a throttle, so it takes a few rotations to get moving, but once the assist kicks in, it’s remarkable how easily you can reach the 18–20 mph range.

That higher speed comes from the bike’s Sport mode, which became my default setting. It requires a bit more pedaling to reach full assist, which explains why my smartwatch recorded my heart rate in the moderate-to-vigorous zone if I was riding above 20 mph.) The other modes are Eco (minimal assist, with you supplying most of the power), Turbo (max power with little effort, making uphill climbs trivial), and Auto (which adjusts assist level to your pedaling). You can also tune each setting to your liking.

It has been revealed that the added bulk is also meant to handle rougher terrain. I’ve had the occasional flat tire from road debris on slimmer bikes, so I appreciate the sturdier, all-terrain, flat-resistant tires. Still, the 70-pound frame makes me hesitant to venture too far from pavement. I won’t be bombing down any mountain bike trails, but it’s helpful to have the option to jump off a curb or ride on dirt or gravel roads.

Sources indicate that the weight makes the bike markedly different from the previous Turbo Vado we reviewed; this isn’t a bike I’d want to ride without assistance. Even the Eco mode, which you’d have to use exclusively to get the bike’s purported 150-km (93-mile), five-hour range, felt a bit sluggish compared to the more powerful modes I preferred. Specialized also sells a 280-Whr range extender, but at $700, it feels like overkill.

The RockShox Psylo suspension fork, with 120 mm of travel, also made this the smoothest-riding e-bike I’ve tested. Other e-bikes I’ve ridden have felt stiff over even small bumps in the road, but the Evo’s bounciness made hitting bumps feel like a nice change of pace. I used to be scared of going over a curb, and that’s no longer the case. The 40 mm dropper seatpost is another nice feature, giving riders a bit of travel and letting them lower the seat to make it easier to touch the ground when stopped or dismounting.

Credit: Specialized Credit: Specialized.

While other e-bikes I’ve owned initially offered good range, storing them in colder weather has been an concern for their longevity.

So I’m grateful that Specialized made the downtube battery removable. Being able to store the battery in my house helps since I keep my bikes in an outdoor shed—I no longer have to worry about it sitting in freezing temperatures. A full charge takes four hours, though you can tweak the battery to cap charging at 80 percent to further extend its life.

The other electric components are nice, too. On the Evo 5.0 I rode, a touchscreen lets you cycle through ride data, including your speed, estimated range remaining, and power assistance level. The front light even comes with low-beam (450 lumens) and high-beam (805 lumens) settings, making my night rides more visible.

If I have any complaints about my time with this bike, they boil down to two things. First, it’s incredibly heavy, making it difficult for many people to take up stairs. Second, the convenience of riding at high speed and making quick journeys has left my road bike gathering dust unless I’m specifically going out for a workout (and those are harder now that I’m so accustomed to riding the Evo). That’s more of a personal matter than a mark against the bike, though. It’s fun to ride, but maybe at the cost of consistent manual pedaling.

According to recent reports, and then there’s the cost. I tested the Evo 5.0 ($5,200), which sits between the 4.0 ($4,500) and 6.0 ($7,000) in terms of cost, performance, and features. At $5,200, though, I would’ve liked to see a phone mount on the 5.0, which is a common enough feature on less-expensive bikes.

Those prices make securing the bike even more important, and Specialized offers a few safety features to thwart theft. As mentioned, you can remove the battery, lock the back wheel, and disable the power system; there’s also Apple Find My integration if the bike ever escapes your purview (a bummer if you use Android, though).

In all, Specialized has upgraded the e-bike experience enough for me to want to upgrade, though the price makes me blanch a bit. Maybe I can subsidize a purchase by selling an older e-bike.

  • Sources indicate that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation of a router model made by Hewlett-Packard Enterprise-owned Juniper Networks, which was part of its modernization efforts.
  • It has been revealed that if you'll recall, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on old hardware the first time he spoke about the event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The router malfunctioned and flooded other routers with data, prompting the FAA to order the ground stop.

Sources indicate that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation of a router model made by Hewlett-Packard Enterprise-owned Juniper Networks, which was part of its modernization efforts. As The Upcoming York Times reports, the agency believes the router played a major role in the glitch that caused it to order a ground stop for all flights in the US on November 13. In addition to suspending new installations, it has also disabled more than 60 routers that had already been installed.

It has been revealed that if you'll recall, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on old hardware the first time he spoke about the event. But Duffy revealed a day later that the matter was connected to the modernization of America's aviation facilities.

Industry observers note that he mentioned a contractor from tech company L3Harris was working on switching telecommunication lines from old copper wires to fiber and on installing the newly introduced router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas. That router started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system with data. Another router in Amarillo, Texas had also gone haywire, and the FAA responded by disabling both of them.

The agency said the router was tested for a year before installations started. "Sixty-eight times it worked well," he sad at a news conference. "This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network." In aviation, routers are used to transmit data, including radar feeds, flight plans and weather information.

Despite knowing that it was the router that caused the concern, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford remarked they still don't know what triggered it. The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee's Democratic members are urging the agency to find out why it had malfunctioned. They also asked the FAA to report to Congress on how it's going to prevent the same thing from happening in the future.

According to recent reports, duffy said he was told by national security agencies that the issue wasn't caused by a cyberattack, but he still asked the FBI to be part of the team analyzing the router from Arkansas. The Transport Secretary has also renewed his calls for Congress to approve an additional $50 billion in funding to modernize America's air traffic control system. "I would just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes," he said. "We do have to get this work done. Otherwise, staying on the old system for longer is going to mean more risk as opposed to fixing the system, and you're going to reduce the risk.".

If the Aboriginal woman had been checked at regular intervals as required, her ‘excess consumption of water’ would have been prevented, inquest finds.

The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.

Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.

State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan ruled on Thursday that her death was caused by low blood sodium levels resulting from excessive water consumption and complications of schizoaffective disorder.

“I’m confident in finding that Tammy’s death was preventable,” O’Sullivan said.

Industry observers note that the mother of five had been taken into custody on remand 11 days earlier, after being charged with shoplifting offences, but didn’t disclose her mental health issues to police. Police also didn’t double-check her answers about her health, despite the fact she had attended a police station two weeks earlier and told them she heard her neighbour talking in her head.

O’Sullivan found there had been a missed opportunity to recognise the mental health challenges that were present, and to potentially divert Shipley away from the criminal justice system.

When she appeared in a local court over the shoplifting charges the next day, the magistrate was not told she had been refused bail on other charges, so made orders they thought would secure her release.

“There was a clear systems failure,” O’Sullivan found.

Shipley should have been continually monitored – both physically and electronically – after twice attempting self-harm in custody.

It was a serious failure that this had not been done, O’Sullivan noted.

“If observations had been carried out at the intervals required, it was likely that Tammy’s excess consumption of water would have been … prevented,” she said.

She deemed it unsatisfactory that Shipley had not been seen by a psychiatrist or mental health nurse at any point during the 11 days before her death.

She added that Shipley should have received medical care from the time she started vomiting, after 10am on the day of her death. Instead, she stated, Shipley experienced seizures shortly before noon and was seen lying face down on the floor of her cell around an hour later.

A period of 23 minutes lapsed between when she was first seen lying on the ground and the commencement of resuscitation attempts, which the coroner found was unacceptable.

One corrective services officer had hastily closed the door to her cell after smelling faeces in the room earlier in the day.

“It was completely inappropriate that Tammy, who was known to be suffering a mental health condition, was left in that condition in her cell,” O’Sullivan noted.

O’Sullivan made 10 recommendations to NSW police, Corrective Services NSW and Justice Health, including a review of the “austere and depressing” unit in which Shipley was held, which was intended to be a therapeutic space but left the coroner gravely concerned.

She also recommended regular monitoring of footage inside the jail and improved maintenance and cross-checking of records related to mental health conditions.

The coroner acknowledged the jail had already made changes after Shipley’s death.

Outside the court, Shipley’s mother, Vicki, said she hoped the findings would force the system to assess how people are treated.

“I honestly thought that at this stage of our country’s development, we have moved past how convicts were treated,” she said.

“The system – every system – eventually caused trauma to my daughter, until eventually it killed her.”.

Vickey Shipley urged the NSW government to quickly implement the recommendations.

“If they’re not made, there will be some other family standing here doing exactly the same thing that I am,” she said.

“All too often we hear the cry: ‘There’s not enough money.’.

Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA.
  • In a recent development, myMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning.
  • “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

In a recent development, myMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”.

Industry observers note that in an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”.

Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

According to recent reports, since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”.

But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi, a mobile simulation that was first unveiled in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

It has been revealed that now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency. Until now, that company has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing claims the firm’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to significant tech surveillance.

“Meta knows what you click,” the company writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”.

Industry observers note that wright noted the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research company” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.

“Right now AI has opened a vast fresh design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright noted.

It would act as a sovereign city state free from things like laws and governments.

Oculus founder and Oxytocin booster Palmer Luckey is touting a newly introduced project that combines some of his favorite things like wacky projects and libertarianism. SLAB is an informal proposal for a floating "seastead" designed to last a thousand years that would act as a sovereign state to avoid pesky laws that "cripple" corporations, Luckey stated.

According to recent reports, an initial AI render depicts a massive artificial island built high above the sea with what looks like office buildings, apartments, refineries... and is that a data center at the top left?

"At a time when most of the seasteading community wanted to escape the US and smoke pot, this was the one project explicitly designed to make America stronger, a relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations," Luckey wrote in a post that must be read to be believed.

Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.

In a recent development, the goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,... pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF.

— Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026.

You may have questions like "wtf is seasteading" and "isn't this just a floating AI data center?" The idea with seasteading is that if you build a floating structure far enough out in the ocean, you can create your own city-state and make whatever laws you want. The concept has been touted for years by several tech bros including Peter Thiel and Joe Lonsdale. However, the only real seastead you may have heard about was Sea Island that the piracy site Pirate Bay eyed at one point as a base of operations.

Recent findings suggest that "The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining [and] chemical engineering," said Luckey. "[W]hile it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion.".

According to recent reports, that raises even more questions! Like, why is Luckey talking about manifest destiny? And what kind of medical research needs to be done at sea beyond the reach of laws? In any case, Luckey, who runs the defense contract firm Anduril and looks on breeding military dogs, stated he wanted to get this SLAB info out now as he was being asked about it by reporters (who later identified themselves as Liz Hoffman and Reed Albergotti, both from Semafor).

Palmer noted that the journalists "plan on calling SLAB my new floating AI datacenter project." However, he offered a riposte that may be the most cringe thing you'll read today: "It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet.".
